extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, philosophy of science, and scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and principles for understanding, performing, and judging inductive (inverse) inference in scientific and logical investigation. Covers nature of inference, methods of discovering laws from data, common difficulties, and techniques to secure inductive conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inference explicates implicit knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Inference never does more than explicate, unfold, or develop the information contained in certain premises or facts; it does not create new truth but renders explicit what was implicitly present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted formulation: 'Reasoning is the showing out explicitly that a proposition not granted or supposed, is implicitly contained in something different, which is granted or supposed.' Examples: unfolding properties of a circle; reasoning transmutes and throws the same matter into a new form rather than creating it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of relation between propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Two apparently different propositions may be related in four ways: (1) tautologous/identical, (2) grammatically related, (3) equivalents in qualitative and quantitative form, (4) logically inferrible (different classes/relations but same knowledge).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: 'Victoria is the Queen of England' (tautologous with reversed order); 'table of wood' vs 'wooden table' (grammatical); qualitative/quantitative transforms (mortality belongs to all men vs all men are mortals); and true logical inference when classes change, e.g., 'All men are mortal' → 'All immortals are not-men.' Use this taxonomy to decide when a change is merely linguistic vs when it is a logical transformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate grammatical change from logical transformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether a change of expression is merely grammatical (no logical difference) or constitutes a real logical inference (determination of relations between different classes of objects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations: 'table of wood' vs 'wooden table' (no logical difference); compare 'All men are mortal' to 'No men are not mortal' — uncertain if purely grammatical. Consider whether the change determines relations between different classes (e.g., moving from 'all men are mortal' to 'all immortals are not-men' is a true logical inference).

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction is the inverse of deduction and is tentative
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction (inference from particulars to general laws) is the inverse and often far more difficult than deduction; inductive conclusions are tentative and require exceptional skill to obtain reliably.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogies and examples: labyrinths (entering easy, leaving hard), factorization vs multiplication, integration vs differentiation. Induction often requires repeated trials and is inherently tentative in complex cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inductive discovery methods: trial, exhaustive testing, and use of deduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery of laws from data is achieved either by exhaustive trial of many supposed laws or by careful contemplation guided by remembering cases where similar effects followed from known laws; the process relies on repeated trial and application of deduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: deciphering a cipher (no direct method; use probability and trial), factoring large numbers (try divisors), use of Sieve of Eratosthenes (systematic precomputation). Emphasises reliance on probability, previous knowledge, and systematic trials rather than a single infallible rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove class identities by decomposition and substitution
rubrics_metrics.description: To infer that a class A implies property X (A = AX), decompose A into exhaustive alternatives (A = B ∨ C ∨ ...), prove each alternative implies X (B = BX, C = CX, ...), then substitute to derive A = AX.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Symbolic guidance shown in text: from A = B ∨ C ∨ ... and B = BX, C = CX, ... one derives A = AX by substitution. Useful pattern for proving universal properties by exhausting and checking alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove a proposition and/or its equivalent to strengthen inductive support
rubrics_metrics.description: When dealing with probabilistic inference, proving both a proposition and its logical equivalent (e.g., A = AB and not-B ⇒ not-A) increases the area of observation and strengthens support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: proving 'all electric substances are nonconductors' by reflecting that 'all good conductors do not retain electric excitation.' In probabilistic contexts, aiming to collect evidence for both the original form and its equivalent is recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide class into exhaustive subclasses and prove the law for each
rubrics_metrics.description: If a class A can be partitioned exhaustively into subclasses, prove the law for each subclass separately to conclude the law holds for A as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: show Carnot's thermodynamic law holds for solids, liquids, and gases individually to infer it holds for all substances; show planets' properties by proving them for each planetary subclass. Requires the division to be exhaustive and mutually exclusive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for exceptions and anomalous cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognise, record, and classify real or apparent exceptions to generalisations; anomalies must be considered and may require special treatment rather than discarding the general law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: diamonds are combustible though gems typically are not; metals can be transparent in very thin films; many profound laws have non-universal exceptions (e.g., thermal expansion exceptions). The text notes a later chapter will classify anomalous cases; in the meantime, express exceptions consistently in notation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction of partial identities (A = AB) as common scientific inference
rubrics_metrics.description: Most scientific inductions establish that all objects having properties A also have properties B (A = AB) by assembling (mentally or physically) instances of A and observing whether B is present in each.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method: collect the members of class A and test/observe presence of B in each. Examples: planets (objects moving rapidly) are not scintillating; vegetable substances contain carbon and hydrogen; many scientific truths are of this A = AB form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cognitive constraints require successive comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the human mind can hold only a few ideas at once, comparisons of large groups must be broken into successive acts (partial comparisons) when establishing identities or correspondences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: verifying long anagrams or that two long lists are identical requires pairwise strike-off or successive checks; proof of class identity often consists in establishing two partial identities (A = AB and B = AB) which together imply A = B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use memory, prior results, and analogies to guide induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful induction often depends on recalling known laws, previous problem solutions, or typical forms, using these memories to suggest candidate laws to test against data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: solving integration problems by remembering differentiation results; using knowledge of customary cipher forms; the inductive process 'rests entirely on the principles of probability and logical induction' guided by experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction often requires peculiar skill or tact
rubrics_metrics.description: The process of induction is an art requiring particular tact or skill; a few individuals attain great success where most would struggle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples: Wallis and Wheatstone as successful decypherers. Implies evaluation of inductive work should consider practitioner skill and ingenuity, not only method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discriminate qualitative versus quantitative expression and note when inference applies
rubrics_metrics.description: Passing between qualitative and quantitative modes of expressing a proposition may be only a change of form, but inference enters when the transformation determines relations between classes (e.g., asserting a class is empty).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'mortality belongs to all men' vs 'all men are mortals' (no change), but inferring 'the class of immortal men is zero' involves genuine inference. Use caution in treating mere reformulations as inferential steps.
